en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huihai Xin of Huanglong, Part One:
Opening the Hall upon Taking Residence at Yunyan. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the time before the awakening flower has bloomed; what of the matter when the awakening flower blooms?
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Look! The monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then..."
The Yang [principle] intersects with the auspicious season; a branch of glory bursts forth. The Master said, "Having eyes, yet being as if blind.
The monk lifted up his sitting mat and said, "What can be done about this? The Master said, "Go out and take care of it yourself."

The Master then said: "Though questions and answers may range freely across all directions, their principle returns to a single thread. The questioner is like a thunderclap or a rolling bolt of lightning; the respondent is like jade turning or pearls revolving.
Every word reveals the ultimate truth; every sentence conforms to the source. Yet even this is but a tangle of oral transmission and mental instruction.
Within the gate of the Patriarchs, none of these are of any use. Why? Because within the gate of the Patriarchs, everything is perfectly complete, identical to the great void."

There is no lack or deficiency; it is simply due to grasping and rejecting that one falls short. Thus, while True Suchness (Tathatā) is motionless, its dynamic function operates within the three realms.
The ultimate principle transcends all names, yet its name flows throughout the four heavens. From antiquity to the present, there has never been an interval;
throughout the mundane and supramundane worlds, it continues unceasingly from moment to moment. Since these moments do not cease, it is like the great solar disc, shining everywhere upon the heavens.
Below. When the sun rises, its light pervades the world, yet empty space has never been bright. When the sun sets, darkness pervades the world, yet empty space has never been dark.
Seeing today, it does not abide in the past; day and night unfold and contract, light comes and darkness goes, darkness departs and light arrives.
Furthermore, how can one explain the principle of that which is neither bright nor dark? Even if you were to...
What has been said here is straightforward and clear, yet it is still only half-raised; it is not yet the time of the full raising.
But tell me, what is the time of the full raising? "The fire burns at the bottom of the sea, reaching across the azure peaks;
let the great sun shine through the midnight hours."

I invite the Head Seat to ascend the hall. Amidst the dense forest of trees, we shall select the *qizi* and *zizi* for timber; among the scattered stones, we prize those carved into *qiong* and *yao*.
To obtain *qiong* and *yao* is to possess the ultimate treasure; to acquire *qizi* and *zizi* is to gain excellent material. In carving and selecting, how could one dread toil?
It must first enter our hands before it can satisfy the heart. Venerable Head Seat, you are a fine trunk in the Zen grove, a wondrous blossom in the garden of *nai*.
As for his demeanor, the assembly deliberated and, by common consent, requested that he be appointed as the Head Seat (Shouzuo). Although he was previously invited, we observed his humble refusal.

Today we seek his counsel once more; we hope he will graciously grant his word. Do you all understand? One whose wondrous faculty penetrates the profound pivot unfurls and rolls up according to the occasion—this is called adaptability.
Ascending the hall, he broke his staff and said, "With what will you climb mountains and cross waters?
He set aside his bowl, spoon, and chopsticks and said, "With what will you eat porridge and rice? It would be better to go to the crossroads and cast lots east and west.
If you suddenly hit upon it, then all of you will have the credit; if you do not hit upon it, it cannot be blamed on Yunyan."

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following dialogue between Grand Officer Lu Xuan and Nanquan. During their conversation, the Grand Officer said, "Master Zhao says, 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I;
the myriad things are one body with me. How truly strange!

Nanquan pointed to a flower in the courtyard and called out to the Grand Officer, saying, "When people see this single stalk of flower, it is like being in a dream. The Master said, "To raise [this case]..."
Easy to see, yet difficult to realize; sharing the same root as heaven and earth, yet how vast and indistinct! Nanquan points it out: the light is like a dream.
Facing this, rely on you gentlemen to examine it closely.
Ascending the hall, he raised an anecdote: A monk asked Lingshu, "What is the master’s house style? Lingshu said, "A field for a thousand years..."
"Eight hundred owners. A monk asked, "What is meant by 'a field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners'? Lingshu said, "The dilapidated house has no one to repair it.
The Master said, "Lingshu’s family is ruined and its members scattered; the father goes south and the son goes north.
Now, if someone asks Yunyan, 'What is the patriarchal style of your monastery? tell them: 'When Mr. Zhang drinks wine, Mr. Li gets drunk.'"
Again he asked: "What is the meaning of the saying, 'When Lord Zhang drinks wine, Lord Li gets drunk'? [He replied: "Let the vast ocean change as it may; I shall never communicate this for you.

Entering the hall, he cited Guo'an’s instruction to the assembly, saying: "For those who have not yet attained realization, there is a constant sense of being overwhelmed and pressed down. Even if..."
Even those who have attained realization and clearly know where they are going remain in a state of restless agitation.
Yunmen asked the Head Seat, "Just now the Master said that those who have not yet realized are in a state of restless agitation, and those who have realized are also in a state of restless agitation.
What is the meaning of this? The Head Seat replied, "Restless agitation. Yunmen said, "The Head Seat is here!"
"This head is white and the teeth are yellow; yet you speak such words. The Head Seat asked, "What about you, Senior Monk?
Yunmen said, "If you wish to speak, you may; if you see, then you see. If you do not see, do not speak recklessly.
The Head Seat asked, "As for what the Abbot said—that it is 'floating and frantic'—what about that? Yunmen said, "A cangue upon the head, and shackles upon the feet."
[The Master] puts on the cangue. The Head Seat says, "In that case, there is no Buddha-dharma. Yunmen says, "This is the realm of great beings such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The Master says: "Yunmen uses an awl to plant a tree; the Head Seat uses a knife to carve empty space.
Even if one were to employ both the awl and the knife together, one would still not escape having a collar around one's head and shackles upon one's feet."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited the case of the scholar Zhang Zhuo, who was reading the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas* and asked Zen Master Cen:

"I see the names of the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, but I do not know in what lands they dwell. Cen said, "After Cui Hao inscribed his poem at the Yellow Crane Tower, have you, scholar, ever composed one yourself?
Zhuo said, "I have not yet composed one. Cen said, "If you have nothing else to do, you might as well compose a verse."
The Master said: "At the Yellow Crane Tower, during the time of the Dharma-battle, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas raised their banners of victory.
Since he has no land, where does he dwell? He has left behind a single poem of great talent."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: One day, a strange monk arrived at Yangshan while traveling through the air. He paid his respects and stood waiting. Yangshan asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
The monk replied, "This morning I left West India. Yangshan said, "Why did it take you so long to arrive? The monk said, "I was traveling among the mountains and enjoying the waters.
Yangshan said, "Your supernatural powers and wondrous functions are indeed not lacking, O Reverend, but as for the Buddha-dharma, you must still look to me, the old monk. The monk—
The monk said, "I have come specifically to the Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, yet I have instead encountered a minor Śākyamuni.
He then produced from his sleeve a Sanskrit manuscript written on *bīṭa* leaves from Western Heaven and presented it to Yangshan. Having done so, he prostrated and departed through the air.

The Master said, "How could this monk have outwitted the great Yangshan? He even produced a Sanskrit manuscript on *bīṭa* leaves to deceive him for a moment. Suppose, however, there were now a truly extraordinary monk..."
Coming through the air—how would you act? He called him over and said, "Wash my feet for me.

On the occasion of returning from the Tripitaka repository, he ascended the hall and raised this case: A monk asked Touzi, "Within the entire Great Canon of the Teachings, is there anything extraordinary?
Touzi said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is this extraordinary thing? Touzi said, "To bring it forth."
Regarding the "Great Canon of Teachings" (Dazangjiao), the Master said: "Touzi knows only one, but not two.
If someone were to ask Yunyan, 'Is there anything extraordinary within the Great Canon of Teachings? you should tell him: 'Yes. When asked, 'What is this extraordinary thing?
you should respond by unfolding the Great Canon of Teachings."
On the first day of the New Year, he ascended the hall and said: "I, this mountain monk, have served as abbot for six years.

I have been sustained by all of you who have illuminated one another through the Way. Since we have illuminated one another through the Way, though space may come to an end, this Way cannot be exhausted;
though space may be measured, this Way cannot be measured; though space may be known, this Way cannot be known; though space may be fathomed, this Way cannot be fathomed."
Since it is unfathomable, how can one attempt to provide a theoretical discourse upon it? Have you not seen the monk ask Zhaozhou, "What is Zhaozhou?
Zhaozhou replied, "The East Gate, the South Gate, the West Gate, and the North Gate. The Master said: "Old Zhaozhou has a secret method:
the four gates open, and the path is thoroughly penetrating. Entering the gate, all is bright and pure; leaving the gate, do not let it leak out. It passes through as a single thread."
For your sake, I shall speak. On this day of the New Year, the Great Annual Festival, I ascend the hall at Cuiyan Guanghua to deliver these Dharma words.
He said: "An echo transmits through the empty valley; from moment to moment, one hears what was never heard before. Indigo is mixed within the colors; day after day, one sees it."
Yet there is no seeing. Since seeing is itself non-seeing, one hears what has never been heard before.

This is called the gate of the inexhaustible treasury samādhi, the gate of inexhaustible treasury supernormal powers, the gate of inexhaustible treasury wisdom, and the gate of inexhaustible treasury liberation.
If one can know and see in this way, believe and understand in this way, cultivate and realize in this way, and awaken and enter in this way, I say that such a person has attained penetration.
The Buddha-mind school: entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Since this is entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, is it the seeing that is the seer, or is it the seen that is the seeing?
If it is the seen that is the seeing, then what serves as the seer? If it is the seer that is the seeing, then what serves as the seen?
If one posits these two views of subject and object, neither is the Buddha-vehicle. What, then, is the Buddha-vehicle? It is—
The Tathāgata is not merely skillful in wisdom; those who possess true wisdom must take the Tathāgata as their fundamental principle.

The Patriarchs were not merely marvelous in attainment; those who possess true marvel must take the Patriarchs as their essential intent. Once the principles and intents are distinguished, clarity and turbidity naturally become manifest.

Once clarity and turbidity are manifest, essence and function are both perfected. Once essence and function are fully realized, one attains great sovereign freedom. Having attained this sovereignty, the spiritual blade and precious sword are ever-present.
It manifests before one’s eyes; it can kill a person, and it can also bring a person to life. If you intend to step forward, you will lose your body and forfeit your life;
if you intend to retreat, you will fail the person before you. Tell me, how do you express the phrase "neither advancing nor retreating"?
After a long silence, he said: "The thousand-year-old pines by the mountain stream gather cranes; The vermilion cassia in the moonlight is the dwelling place of the phoenix."
The King spoke these true words as he entered the temple and ascended the hall, saying: "Neither right nor wrong—this is the sublime principle of perfect emptiness.

Forgetting that and forgetting this, one enters the gate of non-duality. To swallow the rush mat is already to involve discursive thought; drinking water, one knows its coldness or warmth for oneself. Know then that it is not the wind or the banner that moves;
to seek it further is but a vain labor, like the fish and the rabbit. Turning to look at one’s own shadow while walking, one should understand the steps yet to be taken. He then plucked a flower.
A smile. One must know that before the smile occurs, those who wish to meet the blue-eyed barbarian monk will surely awaken to the melting of snow upon a red furnace.
Therefore, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, there is no obstruction above or below; from antiquity to the present, coming and going are no different.
Since there is neither a mind of discrimination nor a dharma of arising and ceasing, the moon of ice is stamped upon the heavens, and the jeweled temple appears at the tip of a hair.
Clearly manifesting the unrolling of the mat and the steep pivot; silently drinking tea, the wondrous intent is entirely without interval, free and sovereign in every direction.
The Dharma King turns at the heels; the Vajra appears beneath a single word. Were one to add further discrimination, one would not avoid the cycle of saṃsāra.
In the past, Transport Commissioner Zhu asked Master Dayang, "How many *jiǎzǐ* (sexagenary cycle years) have passed?
Dayang replied, "Before King Weyin, I forgot the *jiǎzǐ*; even now, I do not record the year. Commissioner Zhu said, "How old is your worldly lifespan?
Dayang replied, "Sixty-four. Zhu said, "How can you be so unaware [of time]? Dayang replied, "The green mountains and clear waters..."
Shui said: "The Great Sun greedily gazes at the moon in the sky, forgetting the pearl in his own palm.
Even so, were it not for the path of the woodcutter, how could one reach Ge Hong’s house?"
Master Xie, the Librarian, ascended the hall and spoke. He cited an ancient case: there was once a monk in the sutra hall who neither read the sutras, nor practiced Zen, nor studied calligraphy;
every day he sat in meditation, looking quite listless. The Librarian asked him, "Why do you not read the sutras?"

The monk said, "I do not know how to read characters. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask someone else? The monk stepped forward, bowed his head in greeting, and asked, "I wonder what character this is?
The Librarian then stopped speaking. The Master said, "This monk sat within his own closed door, yet disaster fell from the heavens.
Had it not been for the Librarian, he would have ended up with Caizhou broken."
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bathing ceremony, he held up his whisk and said, "Look! Look! This whisk has transformed into Śākyamuni Buddha, manifesting his birth.
He emits a great radiance from within the eyebrows and eyelashes of everyone here. Do you all see it?"
If you see, then the eyes are clouded; if you do not see, where are the eyes? To say "seeing" or "not seeing" is like having two heads and three faces.
Ultimately, how will you resolve this? After a long silence, he said: "The nine dragons personally spout water, bathing the entire body."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Mind-essence of Bodhidharma has been transmitted to this day without a single drop leaking and without so much as a hair's breadth shifting.
Since not even a hair's breadth has shifted, how was it transmitted? The precious seal is wondrous in the wind; layer upon layer, the brocade seams unfold."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: Zhaozhou asked Daci, "What is the essence of prajñā?
Daci replied, "What is the essence of prajñā? Zhaozhou laughed heartily and went out. The next day, seeing Zhaozhou sweeping the ground, Daci asked again, "What is the essence of prajñā?
Zhaozhou set down his broom, clapped his hands, and laughed heartily. Daci then returned to his quarters.

The Master said: "Zhaozhou cannot distinguish gold from brass; he fails to differentiate jade from stone. Even if he were to distinguish jade from stone, he would still not have dreamed of Great Compassion."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Damei, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Damei said, "There is no meaning in his coming from the West. When the monk went to Yanguan and recounted this story, Yanguan said, "One coffin, two corpses.
Hearing this recounted, Xuansha said, "Yanguan is a master. Xuedou said, "Three is also acceptable. The Master said, "Xuedou says..."
Three types are also possible: Is it a dead man? Is it a living man? Or is it a man who is neither dead nor alive?
Let those with the eye of discernment try to distinguish between them.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Jia Shan, "What is a 'similar phrase'? Shan replied, "The lotus leaf is round and round, as round as a mirror;
the water chestnut is sharp and sharp, as sharp as an awl. He then asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand.
Shan said, "The wind blows the willow catkins like a ball; the rain beats the pear blossoms and the butterflies fly. The Master said: "Jia Shan’s staff before the eaves!"
The moon is not yet high and bright; at a fork in a narrow path, how could it be the same as the great carriage track? Do you wish to understand the phrase of similarity?
A white egret stands on the sandy bank; the reeds bloom facing one another.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Above, there is not a single tile to shelter the head; below, there is not an inch of earth for the feet to stand upon. Does such a person have a home, or are they homeless?
If they have a home, why is it that there is not a single tile to shelter the head?

If they are homeless, where in the twelve hours of the day can they settle their body and establish their life? The wondrous essence is fundamentally without location; throughout the entire body, how could there be any further trace?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you wish to know the body of Cuiyan, the body is identical to the great earth. If you wish to know the mind of Cuiyan, the mind is identical to empty space.
If you wish to know the seeing of Cuiyan, there is nothing seen. If you wish to know the hearing of Cuiyan, it is hearing what has never been heard. Since—
There is seeing and hearing. Why, then, do you say there is no hearing? If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to comprehend;
only when the faculty of sight hears sound does one finally know.
Entering the hall, he said: "Ordinary people are not sages, and sages are not ordinary people. Ordinary people are themselves sages."
People! The sage is precisely the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). There is no sage apart from the ordinary person; there is no ordinary person apart from the sage.
Only when the conceptualizations of both ordinary and sage are exhausted must you know that there is a path for turning about.

If you can turn about, you will not drown when entering water and will not be burned when entering fire. If you cannot turn about, there are cold and heat that shorten your lifespan, and there are ghosts and spirits [that afflict you].
Alas! [This] envies your blessings. Xie Erhua ascended the hall and said:
"To burn fire within water—those who rely on the earth will doubt this. To hoist a sail upon a mountain—the understanding of this must be rare.
When both principles are forgotten together, one enters suddenly into the profound and subtle. With a single flask and a single bowl, I return to Mount Xiangjiang. This is it.
It is so, yet it is not. It is not, yet it is not. Where white clouds part, the bright moon shines with radiance.
Those who cannot grasp both letting go and gathering in will find the celestial mechanism revealed throughout the mountain pines and bamboo.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A superior practitioner who investigates the mystery must investigate the living word; do not investigate the dead word. Why?

If you can attain clarity within the living word, you will put all the monks in the world to death. If you can attain clarity within the dead word, you will bring all the monks in the world back to life.
Now tell me, how would you express that single phrase which does not fall into either of these two paths? Three hundred and sixty thousand [feet] of Lake Tai."
"A thousand qing [of land]. When the moon is in the heart of the waves, to whom does it speak?

Upon entering the monastery and ascending the hall for the formal address at Yunyan Temple: "A veteran of many battles, a master experienced in war—riding alone on a single horse, I invite you to meet me."
A monk then asked: "Parted within Taoyuan Cave, we meet again upon the banks of the Xiu River. Without traversing either path, I ask the Master to speak quickly.
The Master said: "I arrived here three days ago. The monk pressed further: "If that is so, then dewdrops on the cold pines add to their spirit;
under the bright moon at midnight, the old ape cries out. The Master said: "For now, it is a joy that there is no connection. [Another] asked: "Leaving far behind..."
Yousheng recently arrived at Yunyan. [He asked: "What is the Venerable One who is Immovable? The Master said: "At first he followed the fragrant grasses away;
now he follows the falling flowers back. [Yousheng] further asked: "If that is so, then one can stay and stay; when it is possible to go, one goes. The Master said:
"And why are you wandering about aimlessly again? [Yousheng] replied: "How can I help it? At first I followed the fragrant grasses... The Master [interrupted]: "Stop!"
The student said, "Seeking through words, one wanders even further astray. The Master then said, "Who can discern the true nature of the hidden and manifest school?
Coming and going seem still to involve past causes. You must know that those who return home with white hair are neither people of today nor people of the past.
Since they are neither people of today nor people of the past, tell me, who are they? After a long silence, he said, "In the humble alley, one does not ride a golden carriage."
The "Horse of Form" returns and puts on his tattered robe again.
He ascends the hall and says: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a family raising three sons. The first son is intelligent and wise;
he filially supports his parents, receives guests who come and go, and manages the family estate. The second son is fierce and obstinate..."
Cunning, greedy, lustful, and addicted to wine; he lies sprawled across the streets and alleys and ruins the family estate.
As for the third son, he is blind, deaf, and mute; he cannot distinguish beans from barley and is incapable in every task, knowing only how to eat his rice.
Among these three sons, Yunyan wishes to choose one to employ. Tell me, which one will he choose? Will he choose the one who is clever and wise, or the one who is wicked, stubborn, and cunning?

He selects those who are cunning; he selects the blind, the deaf, the mute, and the dumb. Having selected from among these, one first enters the gate of Yunyan, yet Yunyan himself has not yet been seen.
Do you wish to see Yunyan? The spring rain knows no high or low; the flower branches are naturally short or long.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one says it is so, the monks of the world are not without [this realization]. If one says it is not so, the monks of the world are not without [this realization].
Why is this? It is easy to transform iron into gold; it is difficult to observe people and eliminate their right and wrong."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Earth, water, fire, and wind—through the harmonious conjunction of these four conditions, there is the provisional name 'body.

When the four conditions disintegrate and scatter, earth returns to earth, water returns to water, fire returns to fire, and wind returns to wind. As the four great elements each return to their source, where is the body?"
After a long silence, he said: "The mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the stream water is as clear as indigo.
He then ascended the hall and, citing a monk who asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen replied, "The golden wind reveals its essence."
The Master said: "Great as Yunmen was, he bound people to the realm of objects and killed them there. Yunyan was not like this. When the trees wither and the leaves fall, what then?
Coral branches, branch after branch, like the moon."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Touzi, "What was it like before Niu-t'ou had seen the Fourth Patriarch?

Touzi said, "He served as a teacher for others. The monk asked, "What was it like after he saw him? Touzi said, "He no longer served as a teacher for others. The Master remarked, "Touzi only knew how to live his life behind closed doors;
he was not yet able to extend his hand to benefit others. Yun-yen, however, was not like this. Before Niu-t'ou had seen [the Patriarch]..."

"How was it during the time of the Fourth Patriarch? [The Master replied: "A purple mist swirls and gathers. "How is it after seeing him? [The Master replied: "He serves as a model for all people under heaven.
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Master Changsha Cen, "What is the eye of a śramaṇa? Cen said, "It is so long that it cannot come out.
He further said, "One cannot come out even if one becomes a Buddha or a Patriarch; one cannot come out even while transmigrating through the six realms. The monk...
The monk asked, "I do not understand what it is that he cannot emerge from. Cen said, "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars. The monk said, "I do not understand.
Cen said, "The color of Mount Sumeru is blue and blue again. The Master said: "This monk attempts to fathom the depths of the vast ocean with the feet of a mosquito;
he wishes to bind Mount Sumeru with the silk of a spider. He revolves through the six realms of existence and cannot emerge."
Let us set aside for a moment the matter of becoming a Buddha or an ancestor. Why is it that one cannot escape? The green mountains only know how to grind through antiquity and the present;
the flowing waters have never washed away right and wrong.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: When the Military Commissioner Li visited Mount Gui, the Master was plastering a wall. The Commissioner stood behind him holding a brush.
The Master turned his head and made a gesture with the plaster tray as if to take some mud; the Commissioner made a gesture with his brush as if to offer it.
The Master set down the plaster tray and immediately returned to his quarters. Hearing of this, Yantou said, "Alas! The Buddha-dharma has grown thin. Great!
"Little Mount Guiyang has not even finished plastering the walls. The Master said, "Yantou judges this terminology so erroneously;
he does not realize that Mount Guiyang’s military strategy turned a clever maneuver into a clumsy failure."
Record of the Relocation and Installation at Huanglong.
Upon entering the hall for the formal lecture, a monk asked: "Having left the Dharma seat of Yunyan, you now occupy the Dharma field of Huanglong.
What is the Venerable One of Immovability? The Master said: "The color of pines travels ten li; the sound of rain is heard across a thousand peaks. The monk said: "This..."
[The monk] said, "That which moves is still thus; how is it that which does not move? The Master said, "You only know how to look forward; you cannot look back.
The monk said, "If that is so, the dragon emerges from the cave with rain in its mouth; the phoenix returns from amidst the flowers carrying fragrance.
The Master said, "Why did you not speak this way sooner? The monk said, "The cave is deep, so the clouds emerge late; the stream is winding—"
"The water comes late. The Master said, "It does not hinder one from explaining the principle.
The Master then said, "One must personally reach the very summit of Dragon Peak. Yet, when one has personally reached it, there is no one at the summit.
Since there is no one, who is it that has personally reached it? Do not try to discuss this before the Bimbasara Rock; it is better to deliberate upon the road to Caoxi."

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "One who knows there is [the Buddha-nature] is like a stone containing jade. One who does not know there is [the Buddha-nature] is like a single block of dull rock.
One who both knows and does not know there is [the Buddha-nature] cannot distinguish between jade and stone. These words embody the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. 4.
Regarding the selection of phrases: from the "Five Ranks of Lord and臣 (Minister)" to the hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings and immeasurable Dharma gates, none of them transcend these words.
But tell me, from where do these words emerge? After a long silence, he said: "The pearl sinks into the red water, yet its light remains;
The jade is hidden in the Jingshan mountains, yet its value grows ever higher."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Whenever Yangshan encountered a monk who entered the hall to inquire after the Holy Monk, he would say, "Not knowing.
One day, a monk grabbed him and said, "Whether you have seen [the Holy Monk] or not, you say 'not knowing'?

Yangshan replied, "Even I am doubtful at this point. The Master said: "Yangshan was so ill that he could not save himself; how could he possibly save others from their illness? It being exactly thus..."
"At what time? Is there anyone who does not harbor doubt?
[The Master] ascended the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat. A monk asked: "I have heard the Master say:

'This old monk, during this summer, cast three hundred and sixty fishing lines into the Yellow Dragon Pond, yet never encountered a single scaled fish with a crimson tail. Was it the hook that failed?"

“The hook-tip is not subtle; it is because the fragrant bait is difficult to find. The Master said, “After the rain, the bamboo breeze is clear; when the clouds part, the mountains and peaks are revealed.
The monk said, “If that is so, I have already received the good news from the True Man; there is no further doubt between the human world and the heavens.
The Master said, “It is because the hook-tip is not subtle; it is because the fragrant bait is difficult to find. The monk said, “It has emerged!”
"The body may still be changed; it would be difficult to shed one's entire being to accord with the Way. The Master said, "The chaotic assembly of Chan practitioners is like hemp or millet.
The monk said, "Old Monk, you are accustomed to seizing such opportunities. He then prostrated. The Master then smiled.
The Master then raised his whisk and said, "Look! Look! When the whisk is tied, the entire universe and all sentient and insentient beings are tied at once.
When the whisk is untied, the entire universe and all sentient and insentient beings are untied at once.
Even when it has reached such a state, you must still go to a place where there is not a single blade of grass for ten thousand miles. Now tell me, what is this 'ten thousand miles'?"

In a place where there is not an inch of grass for miles around, he remained silent for a long while, then said: "Suddenly remembering the green mountains, I go back; wishing to see this floating world, I come down again.
He ascended the hall and, citing a monk who asked Shishuang, "What is the Master’s deepest place? Shishuang replied, "No beard."
"The two ends of the lock shake. The Master said, "Old Stone Creek is bald-headed and does not know good from bad. Since the lock has no shank, it has no two ends.
Since there are no two ends, what is it that shakes? After a long silence, he said, "The green mountains have no preference;
the white clouds may roll up or unfurl as they please."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient case: A monk from Silla asked Yunju, "What is it that makes it so difficult to express?
Yunju said, "What is there that is difficult to express? The monk said, "I ask the Master to speak. Yunju said, "Silla, Silla.
The Master [Dongshan] said, "Yunju wanted to see the monk from Silla, yet he was still separated by the sea."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The heron leans against its snowy nest—within the same, there is difference. The bird flies to the white ox—within the different, there is sameness.
Within the different, there is sameness; it pierces through the skulls of all of you. Within the same, there is difference; it exchanges the eyes of all of you.
Now tell me, how do you speak that single phrase which does not fall into 'same' or 'different'? After a long silence, he said: "It is easy to distinguish flour from snow, but difficult to discern—"
Soot in ink.
Ascending the hall, he held up his whisk and said, "Look! Look! Raising it up or knocking it down—both depend entirely on this very place. Even when raised..."
The myriad phenomena of the universe—forms and appearances are vividly present. To push them down? Leaves fall and return to their root; clouds shroud the azure peaks. But tell me:
is it better to push them down or to lift them up? I suspect you are not made of golden teeth; how else could you draw the bow to shoot at Wei-chi?

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Those of the highest caliber who investigate the mystery must investigate the 'live word. Only when one is able to leap forward and strike without shattering oneself before a precipice ten thousand fathoms high is it truly a live word.
If it is not so, then everything is merely a fabrication produced under the influence of the conceptual faculty.
At some future time, within the Hall of Nirvana, your hands and feet will be in a state of frantic confusion. Do not say I did not warn you. He then descended from his seat.
Small Assembly (Xiaocan). A monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'? The Master said, "Life within death.
The monk asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not the person'? The Master said, "Death within life. The monk asked, [further:]...
"How is it that both the person and the object are simultaneously negated? The Master said, "Constantly dying within death.
The monk asked, "How is it that neither the person nor the object is negated? The Master said, "Constantly living within life."
The Master said: "Now, as for 'small-scale instruction' (xiāocān), it is called 'family teaching. What is meant by family teaching? It is like a household that has three or five sons;
[the parents ask] what the eldest was doing today, and what the youngest was doing today—whether they were right or wrong.
When they return in the evening, the father and mother judge each case one by one. It is the same within the monastic community."
Within the monastery gates, whatever matters arise today—whether they be right or wrong—the abbot must adjudicate them one by one.
Observing the present era, the monastic communities have grown desolate and the spiritual capacity of people has become narrow and inferior; it is truly beyond description.
There are certain elderly monks of fallen status who circulate letters and dispatch messengers, seeking to take charge of a monastery here and then another there. As soon as...
Having acquired a courtyard, he immediately selects an auspicious day to enter the monastery.
He further claims, "I am an elder," and enjoys himself at his ease within the abbot’s quarters. Such a person as this is called the dregs of hell.
Nowadays, in the monastic communities, if one speaks of Chan practice, it is indeed difficult to find such people. As for this lot of you here, I see that your hearts are filled with resentment.
Their mouths are full of hesitancy, yet they claim, "I understand Chan; I understand the Way.
They enter the abbot’s quarters and, seizing upon some pleasant-sounding phrases, offer a couple of turns of talk and depart. This is not the true principle.

Furthermore, there is another class of people who, echoing shadows and reflecting sounds, recognize a state of dull emptiness and claim that this alone is the matter. Yet another group says they see light within the void.
Ying: Furthermore, there is a certain class who say, "There is nothing that is not correct," yet they are mistaken. They cannot be saved.

Such people as these are only fit for the comfort of the physical body; do not let them suffer a sudden illness that casts them into the Hall of Prolonged Life, where they will be like a crab falling into boiling water—手足忙亂 (their hands and feet flailing in confusion), seeing ghosts and spirits, seeking shamans here and there.
A physician diagnoses the ominous and the auspicious; he inquires about what is favorable and what is unfavorable.

Have you not seen that our Buddha, the Tathāgata, is the King of Physicians for the three realms and the Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth? He heals the mental illnesses of all sentient beings solely because you do not believe in your own mind.
You have sought outwardly, allowing demons and malevolent spirits to enter your mind and produce all these various views.
Do you wish to recognize your own mind? It is like the sun at midday: the whole world is bright; where else could there be any darkness?
If you reach such a state, there will be no signs of good or bad fortune, nor any distinctions between right and wrong, or good and evil.
You will then be able to sit upon the head of right and wrong and lie upon the head of right and wrong;

even brothels, taverns, tiger dens, and demonic palaces will all become places where you can settle your body and establish your life. This is solely because of the karma accumulated by you over immeasurable kalpas.
Consciousness is dense and thick. Within the mind, it is restless and unsteady, entangled and tangled;
unable to reach true faith, one is immediately bound by worldly passions and attachments, falling into the seven perversions and eight inversions. People of Jiangnan protect those of Jiangnan;
people of Guangnan protect those of Guangnan; people of Huainan protect those of Huainan; people from the north protect those from the north; [people of] the lakes...
People from the South protect those from Hunan; people from Fujian protect those from Fujian; monks from Sichuan protect monks from Sichuan;
monks from Zhejiang protect monks from Zhejiang. They say, "He is a man of my own province staying at this monastery; I shall go to assist him.

Yet, one day when things do not go smoothly, they turn it into a cause for dispute and everywhere cry out, "Alas! Alas! To travel the path in such a manner is to obscure the truth and kill the spirit.
Failing to reach this point leads to killing oneself. If one is such a man, with a single stroke he cuts it off; how free and at ease he is!
But if he cannot cut it off, he is bound everywhere by love: bound by love for form through form, and bound by the monastery through the monastery.
Attachment is called being bound by names; attachment to profit is called being bound by profit; attachment to the body is called being bound by the body.
Why do you not retreat and reflect? What good is there in this sack of stinking skin?
At that time, it was solely because of a single thought of attachment that you entered the mother's womb and underwent the conjoining of paternal semen and maternal blood to become a mass of pus.
When your mother ate hot food, you immediately underwent the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons; when she ate cold food, you immediately underwent the Hell of Frozen Ice.
This continued until you emerged from her womb, where you experienced cold and heat, hunger and satiety, illness and suffering—tormented and oppressed incessantly right up to this very day.
It is solely because you were unable to look back upon yourself that there have been so many such experiences.
This is neither arising nor ceasing. I am born and you die; I die and you are born. Life after life, death after death; death after death, life after life.
One receives retribution according to one's karma, without any rest. Lately, there has emerged another sort of dog-like servant who accepts wages for their labor.

Having purchased a certificate of ordination, they shave off their dog-like heads and don the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*. Unable to distinguish master from servant, nor beans from wheat, they enter my Dharma and destroy it.
They do nothing but wrap themselves up in a whole body, twisting their waists and pressing their hips, brandishing arms and acting wildly, claiming they wish to be great men.
But a great man does not act in such a way. If you wish to be a great man, you must...
Step back! Do not look at me from the front or behind. You are like the lips of a slave or the tongue of a maid—disparaging what is good and praising what is bad.

You speak of how the food and drink here are rich and plentiful, or how the quarters there are comfortable and convenient. There is no need for such talk, O Venerable Elders. A human body is difficult to obtain.
The Buddha-Dharma is difficult to hear. If this body does not attain liberation in this present life, toward what other life shall we turn to liberate it?
You who wish to practice Zen must let go. What is it that you must let go of? Let go of the four elements and the five aggregates;
let go of the vast amount of karmic consciousness accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. Investigate and penetrate deeply beneath your own feet.
Look! What is this principle? Push it forward and push it back; suddenly, the flower of the mind will burst forth in brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
This can truly be called "attaining it in the mind and responding with the hand," whereby one is able to transform the great earth into gold and churn the long river into cream and curd.
Is this not a fulfillment of one's entire life? Do not merely occupy yourself with the sutras, engaging in endless thoughts and words.
Investigate Chan; investigate the Way. Chan and the Way do not reside in the written characters.
Even if you could recite the entire Tripitaka and the works of the Hundred Schools of thought, these are merely idle words. At the moment of death, none of them will be of any use.

Only after the ancients attained awakening did they seek out enlightened masters to sift through the gravel and sand until only the pure, singular reality remained—weighed and measured with exact precision.
It is like a person opening a general merchandise shop where there is no kind of item that is not available.
If someone comes to buy licorice, one gives them licorice; if someone comes to buy *huanglian* (Coptis), one gives them *huanglian*.
One must not give licorice to someone who has come to buy *huanglian*. It is also like having a piece of gold which you take into a furnace to smelt; you smelt it again and again.
It is removed. Once it has been refined to perfection, it is then placed under the hammer and tongs to be forged into a vase, a platter, a hairpin, or an armlet.

One clearly distinguishes exactly how many *liang* the vase weighs and how many *liang* the platter weighs; thereafter, these vases, platters, hairpins, and armlets are melted down once again into a single mass of gold.
This is called the Dharma-gate of Equal Flavor. If it were not so, it would all be nothing but a vague semblance of True Suchness and a crude approximation of Buddha-nature.
Do you understand? Do you believe? Just now, I offered four turning phrases in response to that monk.
In death there is life; in life there is death. In death there is constant death; in life there is constant life.
Use these four turning phrases to test the monks of the world. But tell me, what do the monks of the world use to test Huanglong?
After a long silence, he said: "In his essential nature, he possesses fine flesh and bone; even without applying rouge, he is elegant."
Small Assembly (Xiaocan). A monk asked, "What is the source of Huanglong? The Master said, "Profound and bottomless.
The monk said, "Is it not simply this profundity and bottomlessness that constitutes it? The Master said, "White waves surging to the heavens.
The monk said, "If someone comes who can seize the clouds and leap over the waves, what then? The Master said, "I, the old monk, simply keep watch."
[The monk] asked, "What is Huanglong’s phrase for receiving people? The Master said, "Opening his mouth, he loves to scold people.
The monk said, "That which scolds is the phrase for receiving people. What about the phrase for testing people? The Master said, "Simply recognize the one who scolds.
[The monk] asked, "What is the pearl beneath Huanglong’s chin? The Master said, "It illuminates the past and reaches across the present."
The monk asked, "I do not ask about a drop of water freezing into ice; how is it to be a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace?
The Master said, "Has the Venerable One attained realization yet? The monk said, "This student has not yet realized. The Master said, "A grass-robber has been utterly defeated!
The monk then bowed.
The Master then said: "Profound and bottomless; vast and boundless. White waves surge to the heavens. How can one discern the course of the water?
If you recognize the course of the water, you recognize its source. Since you do not yet recognize the source, let me speak a word of no meaning for all of you.
As for this word of no meaning, how will you understand it? Do not say it is because the Elder loves to scold people."
Is this idle chatter? Is it not merely speaking of worldly right and wrong, or long and short—is that idle chatter?
It is not this principle. As I look upon you lot, you are truly a pitiful sight. At a mere whim, you kick things up;
nine out of ten of you are reckless and crude, doing nothing more than reciting some trivial words and idle talk.
Come! When you are grappling with one another in combat, you cannot even leave. Nowadays, there is a certain class of elders who love to use words to teach people;
it is just like passing a mouthful of rice through three villages in a succession—once it is wrong, it is called slandering the Great Prajñāpāramitā, which is truly difficult to repent for.
Why do you not feel about within your own belly? Suddenly, the illness is there.
Upon the bed, at the moment of death, the breath in the throat struggles to ascend and descend;
the four elements are no longer mobile, and one can no longer speak. All the words one has mastered throughout one's life are of no use here.
I look at this group of yours; not a single one among you is capable of doing the work. When you first arrived, everyone said, "The matter of birth and death is great.
But now that you have stepped out through the gate of the abbot’s quarters, everywhere you go you do nothing but strike [kong-kong].
What kind of fool are you? There is death right upon your head; how will you avoid it?
Lord Yama is not your father—why do you not save yourself? Have you not seen the ancients say:
"If one's clothes are so easily torn, yet one cannot achieve the Way, this is called 'forgetting one's body for the sake of the Dharma. Why do you not look into that? As for me here...
Within, I likewise have no Zen or Way to give to you. I require only that you yourself awaken directly and immediately.
If you have not yet awakened, then silently and in private investigate this pillar. If you can penetrate the pillar thoroughly, you will see the Senior Elder.
If you can penetrate the cat or the dog thoroughly, you will also see the Senior Elder. If you still do not understand, then [look to] the Junior Elder.
I do not begrudge my verbal karma; let me give you a parable. What is it like? It is like the new moon when it first appears:
there is only a tiny sliver on the first, second, and third days, but as it gradually brightens, by the fifteenth night it is perfectly full, radiant, and pure.
There is nowhere it does not illuminate. Furthermore, from the sixteenth to the seventeenth day, it gradually wanes;
by the night of the twenty-ninth or thirtieth, it has completely vanished. Yet when the first day of the month arrives, the moon arises again as before.

It is the same with you all: if there is delusion, one must attain enlightenment. Once enlightenment is attained, one must recognize delusion within enlightenment and enlightenment within delusion—delusion and enlightenment are both [empty].
Forget it. Rather, from the state of non-awakening, establish all dharmas and clearly discern all dharmas:

one is one, two is two, three is three, four is four; this is blue, this is yellow, this is red, this is white. This is called possessing the eye of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*);
only then can one enter worldly dharmas, supramundane dharmas, and both the mundane and supramundane, and be able to blend them together as one.
Sentient beings and Buddhas have been one from the very beginning. One is the infinite; the infinite is one.

A single sound transforms into all sounds; all sounds return to a single sound. In the state of silence where this single sound resides, one lets go and walks forth—this may be called a true man of great character.
Reaching this point, what are the Buddhas of the three periods of time? They are nothing but dry dung-sticks. What is the entire Tripitaka? It is nothing but dry dung-sticks.
What is this "Teaching"? It is merely a rag used for wiping away impure paper.

What are these various great patriarchs and old monks of the world? They are nothing but bed-wetting ghosts. It is simply because you sentient beings fear coming when karma arrives, and fear going when it departs.
Seeing wealth or beauty in a dream, you immediately crave them; seeing someone suddenly appear out of the darkness, you immediately become suspicious. Your illness lies therein.
Why is this? It is simply because you have not yet refined the impurities of the sense faculties and their objects; therefore, as soon as something stirs, you fall into doubt.
You must cause them to become one single mass before there can be even a slight degree of correspondence.
If you cannot yet do so, go instead to the meditation hall and exert your spirit. Sit there for ten or twenty years. If you still do not realize Zen, bring me a knife!
"Cut off the head of the new elder! Although it is so, if you were to sit for another twenty years, the new elder would have died.
Since the new elder has already died, where else would you go to cut? Whether you cut or not, it is because your root-nature is dull;
for now, simply cultivate the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds on the path of humans and devas for three lifetimes and five lifetimes.

Be born as a human being; do not let this precious human life be lost. As soon as you emerge from the womb, you will find it easier. A hundred years for a fool lasts but a single *kṣaṇa*. If you awaken in that *kṣaṇa*, you will become a man of the Way who is free from concerns. Have you not seen how the Immortal of the Five Supernatural Powers asked the World-Honored One: "The Buddha possesses six supernatural powers, while I possess five. What is this one power that I lack? The World-Honored One replied: "It is the power of knowing the past lives of all sentient beings. The Immortal said: "I can know the past lives of all sentient beings, yet I cannot know my own. How is this so? The World-Honored One replied: "Because you have not yet severed the root of doubt. The Immortal said: "How can I sever the root of doubt? The World-Honored One replied: "If you can see the Buddha, you will immediately sever the root of doubt. The Immortal said: "How can I see the Buddha? The World-Honored One replied: "If you can see the Buddha, you will immediately see yourself. The Immortal said: "If I see myself, how can I see the Buddha? The World-Honored One replied: "If you can see yourself, you will immediately see the Buddha. The World-Honored One called out, "Five-Supernormal-Power Seer! The seer responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "Which one of the five supernormal powers do you ask me about?
The Master said, "The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom; which one of the five supernormal powers would not have fallen under his lethal grasp? Take care!"
In a small public discourse (*xiao can*), he addressed the assembly, saying: "The candle on the east side is so bright; the candle on the west side is so dark.
Is there anyone who does not involve themselves in brightness and darkness? Come forth and speak! Is there such a one? Is there? If there is none...
Elder Huanglong has gone off in all directions, upside down and topsy-turvy. This year’s spring of the Cold Food Festival passes, yet the practitioners have heard nothing at all.
Among the tens of thousands of peach trees, which one has seen Lingyun? If you wish to see Lingyun, do not seek him on the branches.
Do not seek it upon the flowers; simply awaken suddenly to your original mind, and it will manifest naturally.
Nowadays, many who practice Zen fail to recognize their original mind, instead taking mere cleverness and sharp wit to be their own capability.
Suddenly, when pushed out by others to serve as an elder, they sit upon a crooked wooden bed, speaking gibberish and answering questions about Zen or the Way.
He replied: "When asked about the Buddha, he answered as the Buddha; when asked about the Patriarchs, he answered as the Patriarchs.
He then proceeded to explain it phrase by phrase: "This one points upward; that one points downward. This is the eye of the Way; that one penetrates sound and form.
Today you understand one case; tomorrow you understand another. You stuff them into your leather bag—when will there ever be an end to this? Others again..."
The Way: when seeing a mountain, simply call it a mountain; when seeing water, simply call it water. Proceed with straightforward reality in all places.
Whenever there is a question or answer, respond only according to the facts. Alas, alas! To speak in such a manner is entirely the view of a wild fox;
it not only buries oneself, but also betrays the former sages. Consider, for instance, the coming of Bodhidharma from the West.

"Not relying on words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood"—how could this possibly be a transmission of verbal explanations or a search for intellectual cleverness?
It is simply that you must realize your own fundamental mind and see your own original nature, thereby forever liberating yourself from birth and death and returning home to sit in peace.
If you reach home, you must know what happens within the house; once you know what happens within the house, then in all places...
When one’s training is matured, it is like a white ox roaming freely in the open;
only then, upon contact, does realization arise, and one possesses the capacity for true freedom. Have you not seen how in the teachings there was a merchant who went to sea to gather treasures?
He encountered a navigator who led him to a place of silver. The merchant wished to gather it, but the navigator said, "This is not yet the ultimate treasure. Furthermore—

They arrived at the place where gold was found. The merchants wished to gather it, but the ship’s captain said, "This is not yet the supreme treasure. They then arrived at the place where lapis lazuli and various other jewels were found.
The merchants wished to gather them, but the ship’s captain said, "These are not yet the supreme treasure. Then they arrived at the place where mani-jewels were found.

Then one sees dragons and snakes surrounding and protecting [one], leaving no opening for a hand to be placed. Reaching this point, it may be said that even the Buddha-eye cannot peer into it, and ghosts and spirits cannot fathom it.
Nevertheless, you must further know there is a path for turning around; only then will it be attained.
If you can turn, then in all places you will naturally stand out in solitary clarity, needing no contrivance and attaching to no calculations.
Seized by the hand of faith, each and every thing is within the center; thus one can give rise to things everywhere and extinguish them everywhere. In the heavens, one is the same as the heavens;
among humans, one is the same as humans; among animals, one is the same as animals; among hungry ghosts, one is the same as hungry ghosts.

Therefore, when one point is penetrated, a thousand points and ten thousand points are all identical. It is like a single drop of rain: when it falls in one place, it rains throughout the world. One...
When flowers bloom, all under heaven is spring. Nowadays, most members of the Zen community merely recognize that rice is made from grain.
